audio_caption: The clip begins with dramatic orchestral music that evokes a sense of grandeur. A male speaker then introduces himself as "Professor Jimpathy" and announces that this is a lecture video for astronomy, chapter one, and that these videos will be done for every chapter and module. The music fades as he speaks.

The audio clip begins with someone inviting the listener to start a PowerPoint presentation. The slide shown is labeled "Chapter 1." A male voice is speaking, explaining that they will take a tour around the universe. He says that we first see a group of distant galaxies, two of them colliding together, and galaxies don't really collide like cars do; they kind of merge into a morph of each other. He continues, noting that the galaxies are two spiral galaxies like the Milky Way galaxy, our home galaxy, and that it is a Hubble Space Telescope picture.

The audio clip features a male speaker discussing the planet Mars and its Mariner Valley, describing it as a vast canyon, much larger and deeper than the Grand Canyon on Earth. He then moves on to the topic of a stellar corpse, specifically the Crab Nebula, talking about how massive stars explode and die, forming heavy elements. The speaker emphasizes that those heavy elements, like calcium and iron, are what we find in our bodies and blood.

The audio clip begins with a male speaker introducing the Orion Nebula as the "most beautiful thing in the entire night sky." He describes it as a star-birthing region, comparing the lives of stars to human lives. He mentions its distance and refers to his prior research on stars in the nebula's center.  The speaker then transitions to discussing the Hubble Space Telescope, its launch, and its upcoming replacement by the James Webb Space Telescope. He mentions that the Hubble Space Telescope was named after Edwin P. Hubble, an American astronomer born in Marshfield, Missouri, near the speaker's current location. He mentions landmarks named after Hubble in the town, including a replica on the town square.

The audio begins with a male speaker describing the Earth, referencing Carl Sagan's term "pale blue dot," and explaining its image taken from a geostationary satellite. He elaborates on the satellite's purpose, including communications, TV broadcasts, and weather monitoring, emphasizing its constant position relative to Earth's rotation. He further explains the orbital period of around 24 hours. He then introduces the scaling of the Earth and the Moon, describing their relative distance and size.

The clip begins with speech from one male speaker, describing the "entire solar system family," including small and Jovian planets, as well as dwarf planets like Pluto and Ceres. He notes that Ceres used to be the biggest asteroid and Pluto used to be the ninth planet, but is now a dwarf planet.

The clip starts with a male speaker describing a "spiral galaxy," referring to "bright areas of blue and white" and "lanes of dust" as the "ingredients to make new stars." The recording ends with a distinct sound, likely a click.

The audio begins with a male speaker describing an image, referring to "a long time-lapse image of the Milky Way galaxy." He speaks in a calm, informative tone, mentioning the difficulty of seeing the Milky Way from cities due to light pollution. He contrasts this by describing its beauty in the Arizona desert and his experience at Kitt Peak National Observatory, adding that one would not see this from Las Vegas.

The audio features one speaker, presumably a man, discussing globular star clusters. He mentions they can have "quarter million stars" and that they "surround the entire Milky Way galaxy," speaking in an informative tone.

One male speaker with an enthusiastic, educational tone discusses galaxies, noting that they can be examined via millimeter light and hydrogen radiation with radio telescopes. He references various galaxies, including the Magellanic Clouds, the Andromeda galaxy, and the Fornax cluster, emphasizing that the Andromeda galaxy is "twice the size of the Milky Way" and heading towards it. He mentions the concept of "look back time," explaining how we can look back in the history of the universe to see how galaxies used to be.

A single male speaker with a slightly enthusiastic tone explains a timeline, stating that if you "take the entire timeframe of the universe" and look at it from the Big Bang to today, certain events would occur in specific months. The Big Bang is described as happening on "January 1st", the Milky Way forms in May, the solar system begins to form in September, and the first complex lifeforms appear in November. The dinosaurs, he says, came on "Christmas day" and became extinct on the 30th of December, before the emergence of "humans" in the last hours of the last day.

The clip begins with a male speaker expressing gratitude for joining a video lecture. Subsequently, a different male speaker encourages viewers to enjoy a short astronomy episode, promotes related videos, and urges them to subscribe to his channel, ending with a thank you.
